Stay in and fight the battles. Don't run away. 
Life is tough in many occupations. I appreciate good dedicated physicians. I am delighted that physicians want more patient engagement and less interference by accountants, politicians, and clerks. But please consider what the rest of us see when you talk like this:
First, there are a *ton* of equally qualified applicants ready to take your place when you step away. I am sure medical schools take attrition into account when they decide on enrollments. Second, regarding debt, if you live like I do for two years, you will pay off your debt in that same period of time. The average post-residency compensation for MDs is about $300K-500K per year (depending on specialization); typical post-residency debt load is about $275K. Third, you have a job for life if you are good, or at least competent. I am glad you have choices--most of us don't.

replies.text: 100% agree. Only 16% of students who intended to major in pre-med graduate college with the required coursework for medical schools. And of those 16%, only about 40% actually are accepted into medical school. You can't count your eggs until they hatch. That being said, there is a high rate of burnout amongst physicians, exacerbated by many things including COVID, EMR charting, and having to navigate insurance denials. Additionally, many physicians are trained to have poor boundaries. A lawyer will charge xyz for each email they respond to or phone call they take. Physicians are expected to give their time freely in these scenarios. And if a physician wants to go on vacation, there sometimes can be a level of guilt as you are leaving your patients behind (though this really varies by the kind of medicine you practice). Most physicians (and healthcare workers in general) must really be passionate about medicine and about helping people to make it through training because of the nature of the work and because of the way the healthcare system has been designed (especially in the US).
